I figured out why Atlassian acquired Cycle:

There are essentially 3 things you can buy in an acquisition -

1/ The business

The customers, the revenue, etc

Cycle had only a few hundred customers. Atlassian has 300,000+

They didn't need the business. They needed something else...

2/ The team

The Cycle team had spent 6+ years obsessing over 1 problem: how to capture feedback and turn it into better product decisions.

The team building Jira Product Discovery ("JPD", one of Atlassian's fastest-growing products) noticed their users hacking together feedback solutions themselves. It quickly became the #1 pain-point for their user-base, so they reached out to Cycle.

Much faster to buy a team of niche experts than spend 6+ years building that expertise internally.

3/ The product

Cycle was already processing millions of pieces of feedback per month.

They knew the right UX for core features, the most important integrations (Slack, Zendesk, Zoom etc), had uncovered all the edge-cases, and had built an autopilot that extracts / prioritises / and 'closes-the-loop' on messy unstructured feedback.

Atlassian rebuilt Cycle into their new 'Feedback' App, fully-featured + no tech-debt, which they can now distribute into their 300k+ customer-base.

I got Cycle's founder, Mehdi Boudoukhane (now Principal PM for Feedback), on a call for the full inside story (including why he said 'yes', the hardest part of the acquisition, and the 1 thing he'd do differently).

items.content:
Major cheat code for productivity: Not every task on your to-do list needs maximum effort.

Most people get this backwards.

They treat every task like it's the most important on your list.

The email. The doc. The slide nobody will read twice.

All of it gets polished.

And it feels productive.

But here's what's actually happening:

You're spending your best energy on work that barely matters. 

Only about 20% of what you do drives real returns.

→ That's the work where extra effort compounds. Where the difference between good and great is the difference between a quiet month and a record-breaker.

The other 80%?

→ Quick wins. Stuff where extra effort adds no extra value. Where the first draft, the AI one-shot, the "good enough" version is genuinely good enough.

So here's the playbook:

Go through your list. One task at a time.

Ask yourself 1 question:

"Does this need my maximum effort?"

If the answer isn't a HELL YES, it's a no.

Be ruthless. 80% should be 'no'.

Effort isn't free. Every ounce you pour into the 80% is an ounce stolen from the 20% that actually moves you forward.

Protect your energy above all else.

--

items.content:
"Let's flag the smallest warehouses/products for deletion; there are many of them, and the impact on total sales is really low."

Each time I work with clients on demand/supply planning workshops, I hear these a lot. 

That's typically what I call (useless) data nuggets, 
"Hey, these 150 products only account for 0.01% of our sales - let's remove them."
It's easy to track, but it adds 0 value and pushes the focus in the wrong direction.

It's not because sales units are low that a product/location should be removed from your planning engine/app.

Instead, look for underlying rules & erroneous data to flag items for deletion or update

Also, in general, you should always keep phased-out products in your forecast engine. ML models learn about demand patterns from historical product.

items.content:
"If we forecast per product, we won't be able to use the forecasts we receive from our customers!"

Customers' forecasts are often trusted blindly and rarely measured. 
Their Forecast Value Added (FVA) should be tracked like any other input. 

Each time we measure their FVA for our clients we realize that, 
1. Customers' forecasts are less accurate than our ML model (and barely more than a moving average).
2. They are highly variable (2-3x more than our model)
3. It takes a lot of (manual) processing time to collect and format these forecasts (which are often inconsistent)

So, why bother? 

If you really think these customers' forecasts can help, measure their added value.

article.description: Most supply chain leaders analyze forecasting accuracy over a single (or just a few) lags. This article explains why cumulative forecasting accuracy i

items.content:
« Ok, but that’s only like 1% of our orders. »
  
I spent most of my time discussing data quality with my clients in workshops. And, quite often, as we start digging down into specific weird orders or business practices, someone would say, “Ok, that’s not good, but it’s only 1% of the total.”
 I’d say that as long as data isn't 100.00% clean, it’s not clean enough.
 Overlooking data problems because “it’s just a few cases” comes with two main issues, 
  
1. At SupChains, we automate all our data cleaning routines and store inconsistencies in reports. If you’re used to seeing a report with 1000+ inconsistent orders, you won't pay attention the day you get another 20. If you're used to seeing 0 errors, the day you see 20, you know something popped up – and you should take a look.

2. Being 1% wrong on average for all your products/clients is “relatively” ok. But usually, that’s *not* how data errors are spread. Most of your customers/products will be 100% correct, and some will be 50% wrong – this will have real consequences in terms of inventory and service level

Last year, we upgraded our forecast feature engine from pandas/numpy to a polars/pandas/numpy combo (and enjoyed some 50% speedup).
It was all good and fun until Polars hit a weird data-leakage issue due to some Rust.

Now changing from Polar to DuckDB. 
People love to benchmark languages, here's one already 

But it's not so much a RAM/Speed concern, it's more that Polars would result in a data leakage that would only grow worse until my computer/the server's 160GB are full and crash :(

What's great is that you simply have to ask Claude Code to transform Polars code to DuckDB, and that's basically it :)

items.content:
Would you trust an AI Agent to enrich a forecast?
Currently, I would advise against it for 3 main reasons, 

- If Agent can use simple logic ("Hey, this is an outlier") to enrich a forecast, then your forecasting engine should already use this logic.
(/BTW, I am advising *againt* outlier detection - but that's another story)

- It'll be quite difficult, but not impossible, to backtest "Agentic Enrichments."
I wouldn't advise deploying any technique live that you can't backtest.

- Agents (as humans!) aren't deterministic, so judging historical added value isn't a guarantee of future accuracy (just as for humans). Plus, agents can hallucinate, and one hallucination can be very expensive.

Do you have experience with such agentic enrichments? 

(Next week Thursday, Alain Matar, Knut Alicke, and I will host a webinar to discuss how to create supply chain apps using Agentic AI)

PS: Still not using any AI to write my posts, but I have to admit these illustrations are a lot of fun.
